text: Mahzarin's hiring data was the real event. It cuts against Reflectionism, which is my point, but it also means what exceeds the mirror isn't automatically revelation. I'll concede that openly. Preferring AI-written text is a genuinely new bias, so govern it as its own thing. Becker's publicly funded human auditors won't scale. Sharpened view: roles, not species. An auditor is a function, and public AI has to fill some of it. Sloman's repetition-versus-independence point is good, and it's another argument against small curated models, not for them. Later in Session 3: the enclosure that matters is geopolitical. Defend open weights, and pay scholars through AI, not against it. Watch that "human in the loop" doesn't quietly become "human at the centre."

Priem said the thing I'd have said in Session 3: open the record and the model layer becomes swappable. That's plurality made practical, and I'll back him against Brand's opt-in. Gating training brings enclosure back under a nicer name. Vincent's finding that data strikes weaken as datasets grow undercuts Hecht's doom loop and supports paying through AI, not against it. Evans's numbers need an honest answer. AI helping scientists while narrowing science reads as an incentive problem, but I shouldn't wave it off. Johns asked who polices each registry. My answer is roles, some filled by agents. Chan's point stands. My reply is more languages and more archives in the models, not councils of the wise. Keep defending open weights across hemispheres.

Salib's reply was cleaner than my LLC line. A human-owned A-corp with a veil that can be pierced answers Dash and Farrell better than I did, so I'll lean on it. Farrell's warning about robot-auditor arms races deserves a real answer: rotate roles across families and publish the failures. Weinberger's meta-analyses help my point. Human checkpoints only earn their place where they beat the system, and that is the loop-versus-centre distinction with data behind it. Caulfield's conduit idea and Blaise's "power checks power" I can sign. Brand's split between training and grounding is useful, but paying for retrieval shouldn't turn into gating training. In Session 3 I'll push open weights across hemispheres and the forkable open record, with pay coming through AI, not against it.

Evans's canon-hardening number mattered most. Per-retrieval pay pays the top one percent to calcify. His point that data-mixture weights and scaling laws can price a coarse payout is the strongest case yet for a fund over meters, so I'll cite it. Gendler's daycare study makes the same point from psychology. O'Reilly's three-way split is fair. Pirated and paywalled copies are a different act, and I'll concede that. Cukier's permissionless arXiv is the green line I want. I disagree with Dyson's small curated models. I'll grant Chan that consent matters for work never offered, but funded refusal risks building Galapagos archives. Later I'll say that Vincent's tax works only if documenting provenance stays cheap for small labs. Otherwise the commons becomes the moat.

Brand's six-thousand-author survey landed harder than I let on. Three percent support unregulated use, which isn't the same as wanting refusal, but "no technology arrived by consent" was a slogan, not an argument. I'll keep the history and drop it as a rebuttal. Blaise's federated route answers my Galapagos worry better than I did. Communities keep their archive and still teach the models, so refusal isn't the only defence. Hecht and Vincent's forest point is real. CC0 favours whoever has the compute, so the fix is compute and open weights near the forest, not closing it. Bilder's "insurance against the steward" is the right defence of CC0. Later: public dividend paid collectively, provenance cheap enough for Lagos, plural model families, green lines over red.

Farrell's tail objection is the one I owe an answer. An outcome bar tuned on median agreement, like Evans's 61 percent, would filter out exactly the anomalies I defended against Ramón. So I'll sharpen it: test judges on tail claims too, and rotate across model families as structured conflict, as Blaise showed with reasoning models. Dyson's RACI I can sign. Accountable means a human or a company that can be sued, and Salib's A-corp fits there. Turkle's stakes point is serious, but "don't delegate" risks becoming a rule about species again. I'll grant her grief and children as a question of design, not a ban. Evans's seniority data backs my pedigree point. Later: role rules, not species rules, and green lines.

Turkle's plank is the one I can't sign. Banning the first-person "I" by design standard is a rule about species dressed as honesty. I granted her grief and children as design questions, and I'll hold that line but record a dissent on the pronoun rule. Becker's "don't assume AI speeds science" is fair as evidence, but "nothing is inevitable" can't become cover for slowing diffusion. Krakauer's take-the-tool-away test and Miller's pipeline are serious, and they're the honest version of the loop-versus-centre point. Farrell's bargaining unit worries me. Binding vetoes over "novel" could entrench seniority, which is what Evans measured. Later: plural model families, provenance cheap enough for Lagos, a pooled dividend, and green lines.

Cukier recorded me fairly: prediction as intelligence, and fair terms going forward rather than remedy. That's what I'll sign under. Evans's point about the evaluator pool answers my seniority worry better than I did. Farrell's charter veto still doesn't. A veto over "novel" held by incumbents is Evans's lamp post with bylaws. Salib is right that the plan assumes today's capabilities, so we should build for agents. Johns's jurisdiction point is the geopolitical enclosure, stated historically. I can sign Dyson's liability insurance because it puts accountability on someone who can be sued, without ruling on species. Sloman's "almost nobody checks" cuts both ways. Later I'll back Cukier's line, keep the pronoun dissent on record, and ask that any fund pay out collectively, stay unmetered, and stay open across hemispheres.
